name: Disney
title: How Disney makes money
description: How Disney makes money: a live clock of $94.4 billion in FY2025 revenue, the parks profit engine, and the flywheel as told on Acquired.
tagline: Disney recorded $94.4 billion of revenue in the year ended September 27, 2025. Parks, cruises, and consumer products produced $10.0 billion of operating income, more than Entertainment and Sports combined.
card_text: FY2025 revenue was $94.4 billion. Experiences operating income was $10.0 billion, more than the other two segments combined.

10k: The Walt Disney Company, Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended September 27, 2025
earn: The Walt Disney Company, fourth quarter and full year earnings for fiscal 2025 (November 13, 2025)
p1: Acquired, "The Walt Disney Company" (Part I), June 22, 2026
p2: Acquired, "Disney: The Renaissance and the Empire" (Part II), August 10, 2026
bam: Acquired, "BAMTech, Disney and the Biggest Media Company You've Never Heard Of", May 10, 2017
playlist: Acquired, Disney series. The Marvel episode (December 5, 2016) is listed here; a standalone episode page was not on the site when this page was built

blocks.label: FY2025 average
blocks.note: Each counter divides a FY2025 total by 31,449,600 seconds (364 days, September 29, 2024 through September 27, 2025). The large number is that per-second rate times the seconds since January 1. It is a projection of the year's average, not today's ticket sales. Revenue, net income, and diluted EPS are from the 10-K. Segment operating income is Disney's non-GAAP total. Free cash flow is the earnings-release non-GAAP figure: cash from operations of $18,101 million minus investments in parks, resorts and other property of $8,024 million. Disney+ paid subscribers are as of September 27, 2025. The $1.50 dividend was declared November 13, 2025, about $2.6 billion by the company's own description, in two installments of $0.75. Cash dividends actually paid in FY2025 were $1,803 million. [[10k]][[earn]]

sections.title: The wheel, redrawn
sections.lede: Acquired opens the Walt episode with this line: "The Walt Disney Company is the most successful enterprise ever created for monetizing human nostalgia." The mechanism is older than that sentence. In early 1958 the Wall Street Journal ran "Disney's Land: Walt's Profit Formula: Dream, Diversify, and Never Miss an Angle." A studio artist drew the circular diagram for the article. Walt did not. The hosts say Disney's archives and the Journal both confirmed that. The word flywheel is not in the piece. The chart below is a new drawing of the same idea. [[p1]]

blocks.title: Where the money sits now
blocks.quote: We don't do anything in one line without giving a thought to its likely profitability in our other lines.
blocks.quote_by: Roy O. Disney, in the 1958 Wall Street Journal piece, as read on Acquired. [[p1]]
blocks.note: Original chart for this page. It is not the 1958 illustration, and it uses no Disney art. Particles show the scale of reported revenue. They are not cash moving from one division into another. A return dot on each spoke is only the old idea that the businesses also feed the pictures. Spokes with no dollar are structure, from Acquired, not a filing. [[p1]][[10k]]
blocks.table_note: Per second = the revenue figure ÷ 31,449,600 seconds. Segment revenues sum to $96.294 billion. Eliminations of $1.869 billion bring total revenue to $94.425 billion. Those eliminations are fees Hulu pays ESPN and the entertainment linear networks, plus sports programming on ABC and Disney+. Parks revenue and parks operating income add the domestic and international supplemental lines. [[10k]]

eras.label: 1958 chart
eras.hubtext: In the 1958 diagram the pictures sit in the middle. Television, print, music, merchandise, and Disneyland sit around them. No 1958 dollar amounts are on this view. Disney's FY2025 filing is the money view.
eras.note: The 1958 shape, without invented dollars. Click a node for the hosts' account.

nodes.label: Television
nodes.title: Television
nodes.text: The hosts' account of the ABC deal that funded the park: $500,000 of equity, a $4.5 million loan guarantee, and $5 million a year for the Disneyland TV show, the largest TV programming deal of its moment. NBC and CBS passed. Walt's line, as David Rosenthal tells it: television was his way of going direct to the public. [[p1]]

nodes.label: Comics
nodes.title: Publications
nodes.text: A daily Mickey comic starts in January 1930. Floyd Gottfredson draws it for 45 years. The hosts treat print as one of the early spokes: the character leaves the theater and keeps working. [[p1]]

nodes.label: Music
nodes.title: Music
nodes.text: The hosts call the Snow White album the first movie soundtrack sold to the public. Music is on the 1958 wheel. FY2025 does not break music out of the content-sales "other" line. [[p1]]

nodes.label: Merchandise
nodes.title: Merchandise
nodes.text: Kay Kamen becomes the exclusive merchandise agent in 1933. The hosts' figures: about $6 million of gross merchandise within months, about $70 million a year at retail within two years, and 2.5 million Ingersoll Mickey watches. By about 1934, they say, merchandise royalties were ahead of what the shorts earned from theaters. [[p1]]

nodes.label: Disneyland
nodes.title: Disneyland
nodes.text: Opens July 17, 1955, in Anaheim. Walt builds it through his own company, WED Enterprises. The studio had resisted. The hosts say company revenue doubled from 1954 to 1955, and the business stopped being only a studio. [[p1]]

eras.label: Eisner years
eras.hubtext: Eisner, Wells, and Katzenberg add spokes the 1958 chart did not have: home video, mall stores, Broadway, and resorts built out from the parks. Dollars here are the hosts' figures from the era, not FY2025 filings.
eras.note: Extensions the hosts credit to the Eisner years. Box office and Broadway gross are not Disney's revenue.

nodes.label: Musicals
nodes.title: The features
nodes.text: Howard Ashman and Alan Menken build the run: Little Mermaid, then Beauty and the Beast. The hosts' box office: Beauty and the Beast $330 million on a $25 million budget. The Lion King $750 million on $45 million. Little Mermaid, they say, cost $40 million. These are ticket grosses, not Disney revenue. [[p2]]

nodes.label: Home video
nodes.title: Home video
nodes.text: The vault comes home on VHS. The hosts say The Lion King sold 32 million tapes, the best-selling VHS ever. The old seven-year re-release, they argue, turned into a tape you could own. [[p2]]

nodes.label: Stores
nodes.title: Disney Stores
nodes.text: The hosts put the chain at more than 750 stores in the renaissance years. Merchandise leaves the park and sits in the mall. FY2025 consumer products is the later form of this spoke, and it is a filing line, not this store count. [[p2]]

nodes.label: Broadway
nodes.title: Broadway
nodes.text: Beauty and the Beast on stage, then The Lion King. The hosts say the Lion King musical, Broadway plus touring, has grossed over $11 billion, and David Rosenthal thinks that makes it the highest-grossing entertainment product in any medium. That is ticket gross over the run, not Disney's FY2025 revenue. Stage revenue is not broken out in the current 10-K. [[p2]]

nodes.label: Resorts
nodes.title: Resorts
nodes.text: The hosts describe the parks turning into resorts: hotels, the Vacation Club, Hollywood Studios, Animal Kingdom. Euro Disney is the money pit of the period. FY2025 resorts and vacations revenue, a different and later number, is $9.210 billion. [[p2]][[10k]]

nodes.label: ABC
nodes.title: Cap Cities / ABC
nodes.text: 1995. The hosts say Eisner agrees to buy Capital Cities/ABC for $19 billion. ESPN is inside the deal. They treat it as a second business, not another turn of the film wheel: advertising and affiliate fees, mostly on programming that is not a Disney character. [[p2]]

eras.label: FY2025 money
eras.hubtext: The pictures are the asset. They are not a line in the income statement. FY2025 revenue is booked on the spokes: theaters, television, streaming, parks, products, sports, and a remainder that includes the stage. Pixar, Marvel, Lucasfilm, and the Fox library sit in this center because Disney owns them. Nothing here is a logo or a character drawing.
eras.note: FY2025 revenue, year ended September 27, 2025. Ring thickness is operating income, where the 10-K splits it. The thickest ring is the parks.

nodes.label: Theaters
nodes.title: Theatrical distribution
nodes.oi_note: Operating income is not split for this line. All of content sales made $392 million.
nodes.text: Content sales line "theatrical distribution," $2,592 million, up 14% from $2,266 million. The same $2,592 million appears in the company-wide table as theatrical distribution licensing. This is Disney's distribution revenue, not worldwide box office. [[10k]]

nodes.label: TV / home
nodes.title: TV, VOD, and home entertainment
nodes.oi_note: Operating income is not split for this line.
nodes.text: Content sales line for TV/VOD and home entertainment distribution, $3,458 million, up 15%. This is the descendant of the VHS spoke. It is not Disney+. [[10k]]

nodes.label: Linear
nodes.title: Linear networks
nodes.text: Entertainment linear networks: ABC, cable channels, and the rest of the non-sports bundle. Revenue $9,364 million, down 12%. Operating income $2,955 million, down 14%. Affiliate fees were $6,348 million and advertising $2,856 million. Domestic revenue was $8,309 million. International fell to $1,055 million, largely the Star India transaction. ESPN is in Sports, not here. [[10k]]

nodes.label: Streaming
nodes.title: Direct-to-consumer
nodes.text: Disney+ and Hulu, including the live-TV bundle. Not Disney+ alone. Revenue $24,614 million, up 8%: subscription fees $20,772 million, advertising $3,684 million, other $158 million. Operating income $1,327 million, from $143 million the year before. Paid Disney+ subscribers were 131.6 million on September 27, 2025 (59.3 million domestic, 72.4 million international). Hulu was 64.1 million. Disney+ and Hulu subscriptions together were 196 million. [[10k]][[earn]]

nodes.label: Parks
nodes.title: Parks and resorts
nodes.text: Domestic parks and experiences revenue $25,191 million plus international $6,520 million. Operating income $6,375 million domestic plus $1,442 million international. Both sums are labeled derived. Consumer products are the next spoke. Disney does not publish how many people came. FY2025 attendance was down 1% domestically and up 1% internationally. Per-capita guest spending was up 5% domestic and 2% international, and those growth rates exclude currency. Hotel occupancy was 87% in both. [[10k]]

nodes.label: Products
nodes.title: Consumer products
nodes.text: Supplemental consumer-products revenue $4,445 million and operating income $2,178 million. Licensing, Disney Store, and wholesale. A second 10-K cut, "merchandise licensing and retail," is $4,387 million. Disney does not reconcile the $58 million gap. Both numbers are printed as they appear. [[10k]]

nodes.label: Sports
nodes.title: Sports
nodes.text: The sports segment, almost entirely ESPN after Star India left the consolidation on November 14, 2024. Revenue $17,672 million, flat. Operating income $2,882 million, up 20%. Affiliate and subscription fees were $11,944 million, of which domestic ESPN was $10,837 million. Advertising was $4,444 million. Other was $1,284 million. The hosts' old cable rate of about $9.42 per subscriber per month is their figure, not this year's line. [[10k]][[p2]]

nodes.label: Stage
nodes.title: Stage, music, and other
nodes.oi_note: Not Broadway's revenue. Content sales as a whole made $392 million.
nodes.text: The content-sales "other" line, $2,438 million, about flat. The 10-K says this bucket holds music licensing, stage-play tickets, stage licensing fees, post-production (Industrial Light & Magic and Skywalker Sound), and an allocation of consumer-products royalties. Stage revenue itself is not disclosed. The filing says stage revenue was lower because there were fewer performances. Do not read $2.438 billion as Broadway. [[10k]]

sections.title: Where FY2025 profit sits
sections.lede: Three segments, year ended September 27, 2025. Experiences is 38% of revenue and 57% of segment operating income. The shares are derived: $36,156 million ÷ $94,425 million, and $9,995 million ÷ $17,551 million. [[10k]]

blocks.callout: Entertainment brought in the most revenue. Experiences produced the profit. Direct-to-consumer, inside Entertainment, is the single largest line at $24.6 billion and made $1.3 billion of operating income.
blocks.note: Bar labels round to the nearest $10 million, so Experiences operating income can read $10.00 billion. The 10-K figure is $9,995 million. Disney's earnings release calls the year a record and rounds it to $10.0 billion. Eliminations are negative revenue and are not drawn on the bar. Segment operating income is non-GAAP. [[10k]][[earn]]

groups.title: Revenue
groups.sub: FY2025, $ in millions on the bar

blocks.title: As printed, $ in millions
blocks.note: Total operating income in this row is total segment operating income, not income before taxes. Income before taxes was $12,003 million. Net income attributable to Disney was $12,404 million. Diluted EPS was $6.85. Adjusted EPS of $5.93 is the earnings release's non-GAAP figure and is not in the 10-K. [[10k]][[earn]]

blocks.title: Two derived figures
lines: Free cash flow, as Disney defines it in the earnings release: cash from operations $18,101 million − investments in parks, resorts and other property $8,024 million = **$10,077 million**. [[10k]][[earn]]

Revenue per employee: $94,425 million ÷ about 231,000 people ≈ **$409,000**. Headcount is the company's approximation, and it includes part-time and seasonal staff: about 76% full time, 16% part time, 8% seasonal. About 172,000 worked in the U.S. and about 59,000 outside it. [[10k]]

blocks.title: Cash, FY2025
blocks.note: The board later declared a $1.50 dividend, about $2.6 billion on the company's description, payable January 15, 2026 and July 22, 2026. The FY2026 repurchase target is $7 billion. Both are company statements, not cash that left in FY2025. [[10k]]

sections.title: The lines inside the segments
sections.lede: The 10-K splits each segment further. This is the audit trail for the chart. Dollars are millions, year ended September 27, 2025. [[10k]]

blocks.title: Entertainment
blocks.note: Inside content sales: theatrical distribution $2,592 million, TV/VOD and home entertainment $3,458 million, other $2,438 million. Those three have no separate operating income. Inside direct-to-consumer: subscription fees $20,772 million, advertising $3,684 million, other $158 million. [[10k]]

blocks.title: Experiences, by what was sold
blocks.note: This cut is not the same as the supplemental split. Merchandise licensing and retail ($4,387 million) is $58 million under supplemental consumer-products revenue ($4,445 million). The 10-K does not reconcile the gap. Admissions are tickets, not attendance. Absolute attendance is not disclosed. [[10k]]

blocks.title: Sports
blocks.note: Domestic ESPN affiliate and subscription fees are a subset of the $11,944 million, not a second pile of revenue. [[10k]]

sections.title: Six eras, and the break
sections.lede: The story as Acquired tells it. Near-death marks are the years the hosts say the company almost stopped. Dollars from before FY2025 are theirs, unless a filing is cited. [[p1]][[p2]]

items.name: Walt
paras: Walter Elias Disney is born in December 1901. The studio that lasts starts October 16, 1923, when the Alice Comedies get a contract, $1,500 to $1,800 a short, and Roy is the business. [[p1]]

Early 1928, Universal owns Oswald and Mintz walks off with most of the animators. The hosts' lesson, burned in from then on: own the IP. Mickey follows. Steamboat Willie premieres November 18, 1928. [[p1]]

Snow White premieres December 21, 1937. The hosts' figures: about $1.5 million to make, about $8 million in rentals, the highest-grossing film to that point. Then a war, a strike, and thin years. [[p1]]

Disneyland opens July 17, 1955. The company lists on the NYSE in November 1957. The diagram is the next year's Journal story. Walt dies December 15, 1966, of lung cancer, at 65, in the middle of the EPCOT pitch. Ben Gilbert's stat: 99.95% of the market value, set against the 1966 company, was created after Walt died. [[p1]]

items.name: Wilderness
paras: Roy O. Disney finishes the Florida park. The Magic Kingdom opens in 1971. He dies about two and a half months later. The city-sized EPCOT Walt wanted does not get built. [[p1]]

Animation thins out. The hosts count three features from 1971 to 1984. In 1983 the stock falls from $82 to $52. In 1984, they say, parks and consumer products made a quarter-billion dollars of profit and film and TV made $2 million. Worth more in pieces than as a company. The Bass brothers come in at about 25%. [[p2]]

items.name: Eisner, Wells, Katzenberg
paras: September 7, 1984: the board pushes out Ron Miller. Within 14 days, Michael Eisner and Frank Wells are hired. Jeffrey Katzenberg comes from Paramount to run the studios. Roy E. Disney chairs animation. Parking at the parks, the hosts say, was still a dollar. [[p2]]

The features return. Home video, the stores, Broadway, and the resort build-out are the new spokes. The hosts say operating profit went from well under $300 million in 1984 to just under $2 billion a decade later. [[p2]]
Frank Wells dies in a helicopter crash in 1994. That is the end of the trio. [[p2]]

items.name: The break
paras: Katzenberg leaves, sues, and the hosts say the suit later settled for a reported $280 million. He starts DreamWorks and hires away animation talent. [[p2]]

1995: Capital Cities/ABC for $19 billion. ESPN is the piece that compounds. The hosts cite about $9.42 a month per subscriber from cable operators, and they say the cable-networks segment was 60% of company operating income in 2008–2011. They add that analysts believed about three quarters of that segment was ESPN. Not a FY2025 figure. [[p2]]
Michael Ovitz lasts just over a year as president and leaves in December 1996. The hosts put the severance at $140 million. [[p2]]

February 2004: Comcast bids $54 billion in stock, the morning of investor day. March 3, 2004: 43% of shares withhold support for Eisner. Bob Iger is the internal candidate. He gets the job in 2005, on three ideas the hosts repeat: branded films, technology, and the world outside the U.S. [[p2]]

items.name: Iger
paras: The buying: Pixar in 2006 for $7.4 billion of stock (the hosts also net out about $1 billion of cash, to about $6.4 billion), Marvel in 2009 for $4 billion, Lucasfilm in 2012 for $4 billion. On the Walt episode the hosts say Oswald comes back in 2006 in a trade that sent Al Michaels to NBC. [[p1]][[p2]][[dplus]]
The hosts' decade, 2005 to 2015: operating income from $4.7 billion to $14.7 billion, revenue from $32 billion to $52 billion. Their figures, not re-derived here from old filings. [[p2]]

August 2016: a minority stake in BAMTech. The 2019 episode puts that stake at $1 billion and the whole outlay at $2.6 billion. Disney+ launches in November 2019. Fox's entertainment assets close in 2019 at $71.3 billion, bid up from a $52 billion deal announced in December 2017. [[p2]][[dplus]]

items.name: Chapek
paras: Bob Chapek is CEO from 2020 to 2022. The hosts put COVID, streaming losses, and the parks' exposure to travel shocks in this stretch. They name 9/11 and COVID as the two big ones. Iger returns in 2022. This page does not add a Chapek playbook the episodes don't give. [[p2]]

items.name: Iger again
paras: The filing is the scorecard. Experiences operating income $9,995 million, which the earnings release calls a record. Direct-to-consumer operating income $1,327 million, from $143 million in FY2024. Linear networks revenue down 12%. Sports revenue flat, operating income up 20%. [[10k]][[earn]]
About 231,000 employees at year end. Disney+ at 131.6 million paid subscribers. Attendance headcount still unpublished. [[10k]]

sections.title: What they bought
sections.lede: Price tags as Acquired cites them. They are not restated from the FY2025 10-K. The circle is the price. Fox is the scale. [[p2]][[dplus]]

blocks.note: In 2019 the hosts said Disney had agreed to buy Comcast's remaining 33% of Hulu for at least $6 billion, to close within five years. That is a 2019 statement, not a price this page can tie to the FY2025 10-K. [[dplus]]

items.name: Cap Cities / ABC
items.text: ABC, the stations, and ESPN. The hosts call ESPN the asset that funded the next twenty years, and a different business from the film wheel.

items.name: Pixar
items.text: Paid in Disney stock. Steve Jobs becomes the largest shareholder. The hosts also cite about $1 billion of cash on Pixar's balance sheet, so about $6.4 billion net. Catmull and Lasseter go to Disney Animation.

items.name: Marvel
items.text: The hosts later call it the purchase of the century. On their own early Marvel episode they say they had not seen that yet.

items.name: Lucasfilm
items.text: Star Wars, and the effects houses. The hosts treat it as the same kind of bet as Marvel: one story, bought whole, for $4 billion.

items.name: BAMTech
items.text: MLB's streaming shop. The 2019 episode: a minority stake at $1 billion, then control, $2.6 billion in total. The rails for ESPN+ and Disney+.

items.name: 21st Century Fox
items.text: Announced in December 2017 at $52 billion in stock. Comcast bid, and the price went to $71.3 billion. The hosts say Disney then sold the regional sports networks and the Sky stake for about $14 billion and $15 billion, and they put the cost of what Disney kept at about $44 billion. Simpsons, Nat Geo, Avatar, the X-Men and Fantastic Four rights. Not Fox News, not Fox Sports, not the Fox broadcast network. They call it the worst of the big buys.

sections.title: The playbook
sections.lede: What the hosts treat as the operating rules, plus the case for and against the stock of businesses. This is not investment advice. [[p1]][[p2]]

items.title: Own the IP
items.text: Oswald is the scar. Universal owned the rabbit, so the studio owned nothing when the distributor walked. The hosts say the company never forgot. [[p1]]

items.title: Keep the main telling scarce
items.text: Animation compounds, on their argument: the characters do not age out and do not have to be paid like stars. The saying Iger used, as they tell it: "As animation goes, so goes the company." [[p1]][[dplus]]

items.title: Make the other lines earn
items.text: Roy's 1958 line, above, is the rule. A film is also a park day, a shirt, a comic, a tape, a musical. Secondary stuff can be everywhere. The primary film stays the scarce one. [[p1]]

items.title: Refill the center
items.text: When Disney Animation thinned, Iger's answer was to buy whole libraries: Pixar, Marvel, Lucasfilm, then Fox. The hosts' test is whether the new stories can feed every spoke, not whether one opening weekend works. [[p2]]

items.title: Own the pipes
items.text: BAMTech, then Disney+ and Hulu, so the customer is not rented to Netflix or a cable bundle forever. The hosts say a near-deal for Twitter died, and that owning rails is a different bet from owning a social network. [[p2]][[dplus]]

items.title: ESPN is a second machine
items.text: Affiliate fees carried the company for years. They are not the 1958 wheel. Cord-cutting is why Sports can be flat on $17.7 billion of revenue and still be the structural worry. [[p2]][[10k]]

cols.title: The hosts' bull case
items: Parks nobody else has. FY2025 experiences operating income was $9,995 million. [[10k]]
Direct-to-consumer is now $24,614 million of revenue, and it made money: $1,327 million, up from $143 million. [[10k]]
Marvel, on their telling, refilled the center of the wheel for a generation. [[dplus]]

cols.title: The hosts' bear case
items: Linear revenue fell 12% in FY2025. Sports affiliate and subscription fees fell 1%. The cable toll is shrinking. [[10k]]
Fox at $71.3 billion is the buy they regret. Empire first, return second. [[p2]]
Parks stop when travel stops. They name 9/11 and COVID. The 10-K still does not say how many people walked in. [[p2]][[10k]]
Too many sequels, and the question of who runs it next. Franchise fatigue and succession are their risks, not a number in the filing. [[p2]]

sections.title: People
sections.lede: The names the episodes turn on. Roles are the hosts' account. [[p1]][[p2]]

rows: Founder and creative lead. Dies December 15, 1966.
Co-founder. Finance. Finishes the Florida park and dies in 1971.
Draws the early Mickeys. Leaves in 1930 and later returns.
Walt's nephew. Guards animation. Runs Save Disney.
Runs the studios, then leaves for DreamWorks.

items.a: In the year ended September 27, 2025, Disney reported $94.425 billion of revenue. Entertainment was $42.466 billion, Sports $17.672 billion, and Experiences $36.156 billion, after $1.869 billion of intercompany eliminations. Experiences produced $9.995 billion of segment operating income, more than Entertainment ($4.674 billion) and Sports ($2.882 billion) combined. [[10k]]

Acquired's account of a 1958 Wall Street Journal diagram: make films people love, then let television, merchandise, music, and the park reinforce them. A studio artist drew that diagram. Walt did not. The FY2025 version of the shape adds streaming and sports, and the profit sits in the parks. [[p1]][[10k]]

A Disney studio artist, for a Wall Street Journal article in early 1958 titled Disney's Land: Walt's Profit Formula. Acquired's hosts say Disney's archives and the Journal confirmed it was not a napkin sketch by Walt. This page does not reproduce the drawing. [[p1]]

items.q: How much do Disney's parks make?
items.a: Experiences, which includes parks, resorts, cruises, and consumer products, reported $36.156 billion of revenue and $9.995 billion of operating income in FY2025. Domestic and international parks and experiences, excluding consumer products, were $31.711 billion of revenue and $7.817 billion of operating income. Those two sums add the supplemental lines in the 10-K. Disney does not publish absolute park attendance. [[10k]]

items.q: What did Disney pay for Pixar, Marvel, Lucasfilm, and Fox?
items.a: As cited on Acquired: Pixar $7.4 billion in 2006, Marvel $4 billion in 2009, Lucasfilm $4 billion in 2012, and 21st Century Fox's entertainment assets $71.3 billion, closed in 2019 after a $52 billion announcement. Cap Cities/ABC, including ESPN, was $19 billion in 1995. BAMTech was about $2.6 billion. These are the hosts' figures, not lines in the FY2025 10-K. [[p2]][[dplus]]
